summary: The sole illustrative case (Access Cardiosystems) is a patent/invention-ownership dispute, not a work-for-hire (copyright) case, and patent law has no 'work made for hire' doctrine at all, so it only loosely illustrates the copyright-specific gap the clause is discussing.
evidence: Fetched opinion text: 'Inventorship and ownership present different legal questions and are governed by distinct areas of law... what is at issue in this case is the equitable ownership of the intellectual property, because it is undisputed that the legal ownership technically rests in Fincke as the named inventor.' The clause's own quote likewise calls Fincke 'the de facto owner of the invention disclosed in the '645 Application.' Patent ownership vests in the inventor regardless of employment or incorporation status absent an assignment; there is no employer work-for-hire default for patents the way 17 U.S.C. §101/201(b) provides for copyrightable works, so the case does not actually turn on (and does not illustrate) the work-for-hire 'employer' concept the clause above and this clause's own reasoning is built on.
suggestedFix: Either drop this case as an illustration of the work-for-hire pre-incorporation gap, or add a sentence clarifying that it illustrates a doctrinally distinct point (default personal ownership of inventions/patents absent assignment, which applies whether or not the company existed yet) rather than a copyright work-for-hire scenario.

summary: The clause states the one-EIN-per-responsible-party-per-day limit applies 'regardless of whether the application is made online, by phone, by fax, or by mail,' but the only fetched IRS source states that limit inside the online-tool section, without itself extending it to phone/fax/mail applications.
evidence: Fetched IRS page text: '...Availability This tool is available during the following times (Eastern Time): Mon-Fri: 6:00 a.m. - 1:00 a.m. (next day)... Daily limit You can apply for only 1 EIN per responsible party per day.' This sentence sits within the 'Get an EIN' (online tool) portion of the page, immediately after that tool's hours of availability, with no phone/fax/mail cross-reference attached to the daily-limit sentence itself on this page.
suggestedFix: Either cite a source that explicitly states the daily limit applies across all application channels (e.g. the IRS's phone/fax/mail EIN application instructions or an IRS FAQ making that cross-channel statement), or soften the clause to state the limit as applying to the online tool and note separately, if verified, whether it also applies to the other channels.
